Build Log: The Creative Technologist’s Approach to AI Compositing

I’ve spent the last few weeks deep in the weeds of a specific problem: How do we move AI scene extension from a “cool toy” to a predictable VFX tool? While ML engineers are busy pushing the boundaries of model architecture, my focus as a Creative Technologist is on the workflow. I’m currently developing VFX Scene Extension, a local-first stack for macOS designed to test how we can make high-end AI tools actually “onboardable” and intuitive for artists.

The Strategy: Context Before Pixels

Most AI tools ask you to paint a mask and then guess what’s inside it. I’m flipping that. My pipeline starts with Semantic Logic:

  1. VLM Analysis: I feed the plate into Florence2 to ask: “What is actually here?” It returns a list of contextual objects, Sky, Trees, Buildings, Ocean.
  2. Automated Segmentation: Based on that summary, the system automatically generates individual alpha masks for every identified object.
  3. The “Creative” Hand-off: Instead of a binary mask, the tool gives the artist Ambiguous Zone indicators. These are dashed emerald outlines where the AI is uncertain (like the fine spray of a wave). A simple “Edge Adjustment” slider lets the user push those pixels toward “include” or “exclude” in real-time.

The Architecture: A Three-Process Stack

To keep the UI snappy on a single M-series Mac, the app runs as a coordinated trio:

  • The Frontend (Next.js 15): A custom canvas built for “Edge Adjustment.” I’m using SSE (Server-Sent Events) to stream progress so the artist is never staring at a frozen spinner.
  • The Backend (FastAPI): This is the brain. It handles the SegFormer segmentation and the PyMatting logic independently of the heavy diffusion engine. This separation is key, it means I can refine a mask’s edge without touching the GPU-heavy Flux model yet.
  • The Sidecar (ComfyUI): A headless engine running Flux.2-dev via GGUF quantization. This allows 16GB–24GB Macs to generate professional-grade outpainting without crashing the OS.

Technical Hurdles & Current Testing

I’m currently stress-testing the Local-First aspect. Running a VLM (for analysis), a SegFormer (for masking), and Flux (for generation) on a shared-memory architecture like Apple Silicon is a balancing act.

I’ve written a custom start.sh launcher that manages the health checks between the API and the ComfyUI sidecar, ensuring that memory is handed off gracefully rather than fighting for the same unified RAM.

Conclusion: Designing for the Artist, Not the Machine

As a Creative Technologist, my end goal isn’t just a “better mask.” It’s about onboarding.

ML engineers build the engines, but those engines often feel like “black boxes” to an artist. By building a pipeline that understands the context of a scene (knowing a “tree” is a “tree” before it tries to mask it), I’m trying to lower the barrier to entry. I want a workflow where the AI does the heavy lifting of organization, leaving the artist to make the final, nuanced calls on the edges that matter.

It’s an experiment in “Human-in-the-loop” AI where the “loop” isn’t a technical hurdle, but a creative choice.

Big Picture Studio

Role: Narrative Designer & Game Designer
Team: Big Picture Studio, Carnegie Mellon University Entertainment Technology Center
Timeline: January 2026 – Present

Introduction

Big Picture Studio is an interdisciplinary team developing a 20-minute cooperative puzzle-narrative experience played across four mobile screens. The project explores how everyday devices can function as a shared interactive system, where each phone becomes a modular frame within a larger spatial interface.

Players physically connect and rearrange their phones on a tabletop to reveal new puzzles and narrative moments. As the devices align, the seams between separate screens dissolve, forming a single continuous world that emerges across multiple displays.

Our goal is to investigate cross-device interaction design, using the physical alignment of phones as a core mechanic for both gameplay and storytelling. By combining influences from comic panel composition, puzzle design, and cinematic sequencing, we explore how different media grammars can inform a new kind of collaborative interface.

Game Synopsis

The year is 0.

A lone probe descends onto an emerald planet overtaken by alien life. Beneath moss and fungal growth lie the remnants of a civilization long forgotten. Explorer Naiad arrives to investigate the ruins, piecing together fragments of the planet’s buried history.

As players reconstruct the landscape and its memories, Naiad confronts deeper questions about her own origins and the exile that brought her here.

Process

Our team follows an incremental, moments-based design process, rapidly prototyping interaction mechanics before integrating them into narrative beats.

Each prototype explores how physical alignment between devices can create new interface states. For example, players may slide phones together to extend environments, rotate screens to reveal hidden pathways, or form larger composite images that trigger story events.

These experiments allow us to investigate how spatial configuration can act as both puzzle mechanic and storytelling device, encouraging players to collaborate around a shared physical interface.

Through iterative testing, we are exploring how familiar mobile devices can be reimagined as modular components of a collective display system, where interaction occurs not only on the screen but also in the physical relationships between devices and players.

My Contributions

As Narrative Designer and Game Designer, I focus on aligning the project’s narrative structure with its interaction mechanics. My work includes:

  • Designing the core narrative framework and worldbuilding for the game’s setting and protagonist
  • Developing puzzle mechanics tied to device alignment and spatial configuration
  • Collaborating with artists and engineers to integrate story moments with interaction prototypes
  • Iterating on player flow and cooperative puzzle design through playtesting

My role bridges story design, interaction systems, and gameplay structure, ensuring that narrative discovery emerges naturally through collaborative interaction with the devices.

As the UX Researcher and Producer on this project, I had the privilege of steering both the human-centered design process and the operational framework that brought this educational experience to life.

The Mission: Demystifying STEM through Design

Kicks Lab is a transformational educational platform designed to break down barriers to STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) for middle and high school students. By using footwear, a high-interest, everyday object, as the primary vehicle for learning, we aim to foster confidence and curiosity in the next generation of makers.

My Role: UX Research & Production

In a project that blends live simulations and 3D printing, ensuring a seamless and impactful user journey was critical. My contributions were focused on two key pillars:

1. UX Research: Insights Driven by Playtesting

To ensure Kicks Lab resonated with its intended audience, I led extensive playtesting sessions with students from the LIFE Male STEAM Academy, a Pittsburgh charter school dedicated to preparing young men for careers in STEM.

  • Target Audience Insights: Working directly with the students at LIFE Male STEAM Academy allowed us to observe firsthand how middle and high school students interact with design challenges.
  • Iterative Testing: I facilitated feedback loops that transformed complex engineering data into intuitive gameplay. By observing the students in action, we were able to refine our UI and narrative to better support their curiosity and problem-solving skills.
  • Impact Evaluation: These sessions were vital in proving that footwear design is a powerful “hook” for teaching physics, material science, and safety engineering.

2. Production: Industry-Leading Partnerships

As a Producer, I managed our high-level collaborations with two industry partners to ensure our “Lab” reflected real-world innovation:

  • Ansys: We integrated Ansys’s industry-standard simulation technology to let students visualize the manufacturing and design insights at play in a sneaker, such as stress distribution and material rebound.
  • Zellerfeld: By partnering with the leaders in 3D-printed footwear, we provided students with a window into the future of sustainable, automated manufacturing.
  • Cross-Disciplinary Coordination: I served as the primary bridge between our technical partners and our creative team, ensuring that the 3D-printed prototypes and digital simulations met both educational goals and industry standards.

The Lab Experience

The final product is a blend of digital and physical learning. Students diagnose footwear failures, such as lever inefficiencies or traction loss, and use simulation data to engineer better solutions. By integrating Ansys-powered analytics, we provide a tangible link between a digital concept and a high-performance product.

Looking Ahead

Kicks Lab has been a testament to the power of “Edutainment.” By centering the user experience and leveraging the expertise of partners like Ansys and Zellerfeld, we’ve created a blueprint for how to engage the next generation of youth in the STEM pipeline.

I invite you to explore our progress and view our final presentation through the official project portal.

Project Details:

  • Institution: Carnegie Mellon University, Entertainment Technology Center
  • My Roles: UX Researcher & Producer
  • Key Partners: Ansys, Zellerfeld, LIFE Male STEAM Academy
  • Platform: Kicks Lab Project Site

Through playtesting at LIFE Male STEAM Academy, refined an experience that turns sneaker culture into a bridge for innovation.

Anamnesis is an experimental XR cinema project exploring attention, memory, and narrative engagement inside a C.A.V.E. environment. Instead of interrupting viewers with explicit prompts, the system subtly responds to shifts in attention state, investigating how immersive space can reshape cinematic storytelling. The work sits at the intersection of interactive narrative, cognitive presence, and embodied media design.

Selections and Awards:

Student Labs Selection at Infinity Festival Hollywood, 2025

Student Vision Award, Sound and Vision Film and Technology International Festival, 2025

Development

As the creative director and producer of the project, I led the end-to-end creative production of the experience and executed all narrative and on-screen elements. My responsibilities included:

  • Producing and managing the project lifecycle
  • Directing spatial cinematography and immersive staging
  • Writing the complete branching script, including all settings and dialogue
  • Editing and structuring the nonlinear narrative system

I built and structured the branching narrative architecture and ensured coherence across multiple narrative paths in an immersive environment.

Research

Following the completion of the film I independently framed the research question guiding the project, focusing on how attention-responsive systems can reduce cognitive disruption in interactive media.

I designed the research investigation to evaluate:

  • Narrative flow
  • User attention and engagement patterns
  • Perceived immersion and agency

The project bridges cinematic storytelling and user-centered XR research, demonstrating my ability to connect creative production with structured inquiry.

As an extension of the research, I have made the following video to clearly illustrate the prototype’s design and my research goals.

Conference Selections:

Exploring Attention States and Narrative Engagement in a VR Experience, Siggraph: Immersive Pavilion 2026

Planned CHI Paper

Building on the prototype, I am developing a CHI paper with Professor Vivian Shen and Geoff Kaufman at Carnegie Mellon University which aims to formalize this system and its research findings.

Through out the process I’ve gained research skills including but not limited to conducting comprehensive literature reviews, navigating IRB protocols for human subject testing, and synthesizing raw experimental results into a cohesive academic manuscript for peer-reviewed publication.

The paper frames Anamnesis as a case study in attention-aware immersive storytelling, examining how state-based responsiveness can preserve narrative flow while maintaining interactivity. Rather than centering explicit choice interfaces, the work investigates interaction as environmental modulation: a model that may reduce cognitive interruption and sustain presence in XR environments.

The paper will articulate:

  • A design framework for attention-responsive narrative systems
  • The architecture of the branching and adaptive logic
  • Findings from user evaluation on flow, engagement, and perceived agency
  • Design implications for immersive media, XR storytelling, and attention-aware interfaces

By translating a fully realized cinematic system into a structured research contribution, the paper bridges creative XR production and HCI research. It positions Anamnesis not only as a narrative experiment, but as a replicable design approach for seamless interaction in immersive environments.

Cinematic Direction & Continuity

A central aspect of the project was applying principles from film directing and cinematic continuity to an immersive interactive environment. My background in filmmaking informed the visual language of Anamnesis, including spatial blocking, shot composition, temporal rhythm, and narrative continuity across multiple branching paths.

In traditional film production, directors carefully manage continuity across shots, maintaining consistent character positions, lighting, spatial orientation, and narrative timing to preserve viewer immersion. Translating these principles into an XR environment required rethinking continuity not only across cuts, but across interactive narrative states and user-driven attention shifts.

To achieve this, I designed the experience with attention to:

  • Spatial continuity across immersive viewpoints
  • Narrative coherence across branching story paths
  • Cinematic blocking and staging inside a 3D environment
  • Temporal rhythm and pacing of interactive narrative beats

This work reflects a broader interest in how cinematic knowledge can inform emerging creative technologies.

Later framed a CHI research agenda investigating how state-based narrative responsiveness can preserve flow, reduce cognitive disruption, and sustain presence in immersive systems.

Buffering…Please Wait is a science fiction drama short film directed and written by Samantha Cheryl Lai. It debuted in 2023 and has been shown at several international film festivals.

Overview

  • Title: Buffering…Please Wait
  • Director / Writer: Samantha Cheryl Lai
  • Genre: Sci-fi, drama
  • Runtime: ~13 minutes 17 seconds
  • Production: Canada (filmed in Taiwan)
  • Languages: English and Mandarin Chinese
  • Budget: Around $35,000 USD

Plot/Theme

The story follows a nameless woman who explores a memory device embedded in her brain in an attempt to rediscover a lost identity. As she delves deeper, she finds that the truth she uncovers has an emotional weight she struggles to bear. The narrative blends futuristic tech concepts with an introspective emotional core about memory and loss.

Festival Screenings & Awards

The short has been featured in a number of festivals worldwide:

  • Fantasia International Film Festival (Montreal) — Official Selection
  • Boston Science Fiction Film Festival — USA Premiere
  • The Philip K. Dick Science Fiction and Supernatural Festival — Won Best Philip K. Dick Short
  • Busan New Wave Short Film Festival (Korea) — Won Best Cinematography

About the Filmmaker

Samantha Cheryl Lai is a Canadian writer-director. Buffering…Please Wait is known as her narrative directorial debut, inspired in part by personal themes of loss and identity.

Vimeo

content.rendered:
Before transitioning into immersive media and research, I worked professionally as a staff writer under my name Samantha Lai, contributing to serialized television dramas produced for major networks and international media companies.

I was part of the writing team for The Haunted Heart, a Mandarin-language fantasy-drama series co-produced with Turner Asia Pacific (a WarnerMedia company), marking one of the network’s early original scripted co-productions for the Taiwanese market. The series was reported on by Variety for its international co-production model, reflecting its cross-market production strategy and distribution ambitions.

The series received industry attention for its international distribution model and creative ambition as a 30-episode production backed by government support and Turner’s syndication rights across Asia and the U.S. In addition to writing, I directed a 30-person crew over multiple production days to generate supplemental visual content for the show’s opening and ending sequences, coordinating creative direction and production logistics under broadcast timelines and stakeholder requirements.

I also served as a staff writer on The Memory Garden, a fantasy-romance series produced and released in Taiwan during 2021–2022 with The Walt Disney Company (Taiwan) Limited credited as one of its originating media partners, reflecting a collaboration anchored in mainstream entertainment and international brand support.

More recently, I was a writer on Dr. Lifesaver, a 30-episode medical drama broadcast on Public Television Service (PTS), Taiwan’s public broadcaster recognized for its high editorial standards and quality programming within the national media landscape.

Across these productions, I developed expertise in:

  • Sustained audience engagement and retention through long-form serialized storytelling
  • Cross-functional collaboration with producers, directors, creative teams, and network stakeholders
  • Leading multidisciplinary production efforts under schedule and budget constraints
  • Iterative development processes shaped by structured feedback cycles
  • Translating complex real-world and fictional systems into accessible narrative frameworks

This foundation in structured storytelling, audience psychology, and systems design now informs my work in immersive environments and user research, where I explore attention, engagement, and human-centered experience design.
